title: Britain Is About to Get Its Seventh Prime Minister in a Decade. The 1.8 Million Indians There Are Watching Closely.
excerpt: Andy Burnham is expected to enter Downing Street by July 20 — five days after the India-UK trade deal goes live. His domestic-first agenda could reshape life for Britain's Indian diaspora.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Andy Burnham is set to become Britain's seventh Prime Minister in a decade.
  • The India-UK trade deal goes live just before Burnham's expected entry into office.
  • Burnham's domestic-first agenda may impact the 1.8 million Indians in Britain.
  • Concerns arise over Burnham's inexperience in foreign affairs amid critical India relations.
  • The Indian community faces a £4.7 billion defense funding gap under Burnham's leadership.
Burnham's Political Ascent
July 15, 2023
India-UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) goes live.
July 20, 2023
Andy Burnham expected to enter Downing Street.
June 2023
Keir Starmer announces resignation after two years.
May 2023
Burnham wins Makerfield by-election with 54.8% of the vote.
Keir Starmer is leaving Downing Street. Andy Burnham is walking in. And for the 1.8 million people of Indian origin living in Britain, the transition could not come at a more consequential moment. Starmer announced last month that he would step down as Prime Minister after just two years in office, triggered by the dramatic return of Andy Burnham — the former Mayor of Greater Manchester — to the House of Commons. Burnham won a by-election in the working-class constituency of Makerfield with 54.8% of the vote, backed by a massive faction of Labour MPs looking to revive the party's flagging fortunes. No other candidate has come forward to challenge him for the leadership. If no challenger emerges by the nomination deadline next week, Burnham becomes Prime Minister by default — as early as July 20, the day after the World Cup final. ## Who Is Andy Burnham? The 56-year-old "King of the North," as British media have dubbed him, served as Mayor of Greater Manchester for nine years, far from the chaos of Westminster. Before that, he held cabinet positions under Tony Blair and Gordon Brown. His mayoral tenure coincided with Manchester's economic renaissance — private investment, new tram lines, a cultural boom. He earned national recognition during the Manchester Arena bombing aftermath in 2017 and became a powerful voice during the pandemic, clashing with Boris Johnson's government over regional lockdown restrictions. The Wall Street Journal described his ascent as a "bloodless coup," noting that he and his inner circle — including former transport secretary Louise Haigh and policy chief Miatta Fahnbulleh — have been scrambling to condense months of policy development into weeks. Fahnbulleh had been running what one senior Labour source described as "serious work, of a kind not seen under Starmer." ## The Timing Could Not Be More Critical for India-UK Relations Burnham inherits a relationship between Britain and India that has never been more commercially significant — or more fragile. The India-UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) goes live on July 15, just days before Burnham is expected to enter Downing Street. The deal, which took years to negotiate, includes provisions for tariff reductions on Indian textiles, IT services, and agricultural products, along with a landmark social security portability clause that would allow Indian professionals in the UK to count their National Insurance contributions towards pensions back home. For Indian workers, students, and business owners in Britain, the CETA represents a generational shift. Whether Burnham will champion it or seek to renegotiate elements — as some Labour MPs have suggested — remains an open question. ## Vance Weighs In: 'Something Is Very Broken About British Politics' US Vice President JD Vance offered a pointed assessment in a Sunday Times interview on Saturday. "Britain has been failed by its leadership for a long time," Vance said, noting that the country was about to get its seventh prime minister in a decade. "What that says to me is that something is very broken about British politics and that people are really crying out for significant structural change." Vance, whose wife Usha studied at the University of Cambridge, said he hoped Burnham could deliver that change but acknowledged he did not know much about the incoming leader.
Impact of the CETA
›Tariff reductions on Indian textiles, IT services, and agricultural products.
›Social security portability for Indian professionals in the UK.
›Represents a generational shift for Indian workers and businesses.
›Burnham's stance on the deal remains uncertain.
President Trump, for his part, described Burnham as "extremely liberal" and predicted he would not support further North Sea oil and gas development — an issue Trump had been pushing Starmer on. Starmer himself warned his successor that the job demands equal attention to global affairs. "There's often this discussion — what's the right balance between dealing with international affairs and dealing with domestic affairs? They're one and the same thing," Starmer told the BBC on Friday. Asked whether a prime minister could spend less time on diplomacy than he had: "No, I don't think it is possible." ## What the Diaspora Needs to Know Burnham's domestic-first instincts could be a double-edged sword for the Indian community in Britain. On one hand, his focus on housing, living standards, and regional investment directly benefits the Indian-origin communities concentrated in cities like Leicester, Birmingham, and Manchester. His devolution agenda — giving more power and funding to cities and regions outside London — could strengthen the economic ecosystems where many Indian-owned businesses operate. On the other hand, his relative inexperience in foreign affairs raises questions about how he will manage the India relationship at a time when Modi is expected to visit Britain later this year to mark the CETA's implementation. The trade deal includes sensitive provisions on worker mobility and visa access that will require careful diplomatic management. Britain's Indian community also faces the £4.7 billion defence funding gap that Burnham inherits. Starmer announced a defence plan to make Britain's armed forces war-ready, but a third of the £15 billion commitment remains unfunded. How Burnham balances guns versus butter will shape the fiscal room available for the domestic investments the diaspora cares about.
Challenges Ahead for Burnham
›£4.7 billion defense funding gap inherited from Starmer.
›Need to balance domestic investments with defense commitments.
›Potential diplomatic challenges with Modi's upcoming visit.
›Focus on housing and living standards for Indian communities.
The incoming PM has promised to "set out a new direction for the country." For the Indian community in Britain — from NHS doctors to tech entrepreneurs to corner-shop owners who have been the backbone of British life for decades — the question is whether that direction includes them. *Sources: Reuters, BBC, The Sun, The Times, Wall Street Journal, NBC News*
